# Final-Piece Prospectus

Your prospectus is a one-page commitment to a specific, focused project you intend to deliver as your final piece. It demonstrates that you have thought through the study before you start coding messages or running tests.

The six core components are the same in both editions of this book. The difference is in what the graduate prospectus must also commit to beyond the undergraduate baseline.

## Core six components (both editions)

1. **Title** that names the key variables and the corpus.
2. **One to three focused research questions or hypotheses**, not five and not ten.
3. **Two to three sentence theoretical framework** that names the theory and explains how it relates to the question.
4. **Two to three sentence gap statement** with a few key citations.
5. **Three to four sentence method overview** covering the data, the coding or measurement, and the number of cases.
6. **One to two sentence expected contribution** scoped to what the study can deliver.

Worked examples for both editions live in Chapter 6 of the book. Two model prospectuses are drawn from the working corpus and use different theories to illustrate that the same dataset can support several defensible plans.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="undergrad"}

## Undergraduate prospectus

**Deliverable target.** A feature article (2,500 to 4,000 words) for a public-facing audience, paired with a methodology appendix (800 to 1,500 words). The pairing follows the architecture used by The Pudding and The Markup: narrative on the main URL, method on a separate but linked URL.

**Submission rhythm.** Week 5 draft prospectus (in-class workshop), Week 7 final prospectus (graded). The methods chapters that follow assume your prospectus is locked by Week 7.

**Approximate length:** 250 words. The model prospectuses in Chapter 6 each land near that mark.

**Common revisions you should anticipate.** Most first drafts try to do too much. The single most frequent revision note is "narrow until it hurts a little, then narrow a bit more." See the "weak to revised" worked pair in Chapter 6 for what that move looks like in practice.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="grad"}

## Graduate prospectus

**Deliverable target.** A McKinsey or RAND or Pew style white paper (3,000 to 5,000 words) plus a 36 by 24 inch academic conference poster rendered from a Quarto Typst template. The pairing follows current practitioner-research conventions in which a long-form report and a conference-floor artifact carry the same study to different audiences.

**Submission rhythm.** Draft prospectus by the second week of the first half of the sequence; final prospectus locked by the fourth week of the second half. The reliability work in the back half of the course assumes your prospectus is locked by then.

**Beyond the undergraduate six components, your prospectus also commits to:**

1. **A priori power analysis.** State the effect size you can detect at your planned sample size, justify the effect-size assumption with a citation or pilot, and acknowledge when the planned sample under-powers the comparison.
2. **Pre-registration plan.** Document your hypotheses, exclusion criteria, and analysis decisions before you collect or code data. The Open Science Framework prereg form is the default registration target.
3. **Two-coder reliability plan.** Target Krippendorff's alpha at or above 0.80 on a 10 percent subsample, with a stated stop-rule for codebook revision if alpha is below the target on the first reliability check.
4. **Audit trail.** A defensible record of codebook versions, decision log entries, and intermediate data artifacts. The audit trail is the input your AID Statement appendix draws from at deliverable time.

These additions are not academic theater. They are the discipline that converts a coursework content analysis into a study a journal would accept. The chapter on pre-registration discipline in this supplement walks through each addition with worked language you can adapt.

**Approximate length.** 400 to 500 words. The model graduate prospectus in the supplement chapter on pre-registration is annotated by component so you can see where the extra commitments live in the document.

:::

## Before you submit

Run your prospectus through a feasibility test. Can you actually access the data, given the corpus your edition ships with? Can you analyze it in the time available? Does your method match your question (a content analysis answers what is in the content, not why people feel what they feel)? And have you controlled scope creep until the prospectus describes one study, not a research program?

The prospectus is pre-statistics work. You do not yet need to know which test you will run, what your p-value will be, or what R code will execute the comparison. The phrase "will be compared" in the method paragraph is genuinely all you need at this stage.
